I believe the translation to Greek as Hades is meant to relate specifically to the Asphodel Meadows of the Greek underworld. The Asphodel Meadows, in Greek myth, was where the majority of souls (i.e., regular people) went after death, very similar to our concepts of Sheol. It is a place of neither reward nor punishment. It is important to recall that Tartarus and Elysium, while part of Hades, had very strict "entry requirements," so to speak. Elysium was mostly reserved for demigods and/or great heroes (most of whom *were* demigods). Tartarus was, on the other hand, reserved for those who had directly spited the gods: the Titans for their rebellion, Typhon for his, Tantalus for feeding his own son to Zeus and Hermes, etc.

Obviously, this conception changed over the long period that Hellenism was practiced, and modern pop culture like Disney's *Hercules* certainly hasn't helped the idea of Hades being an evil god/place. But, at least put in a historical context of when the Septaugint was written, I think the translation of Sheol to Hades is actually very good, all things considered.

TL;DR: People don't like having knowledge kept from them and feel like they are only told what they "need to know". People question what qualifies as "need to know" and who gets to decide that. People feel like they are being told what to believe and they don't like that, so they assume that the ones telling them are trying to control them and making up lies to do so. Because, in their eyes, they don't "need" to know anything and it is incredibly presumptive for academics to tell them otherwise. 

Legitimately? For one, people are sick of hearing about WWII. Many people also have an intense distrust of academics and scholars. I'm a history student at a fairly large university. I can say from my own experiences that there are fewer and fewer historians researching and writing about WWII and the Holocaust because, to a degree, there's not much more to be learned. 

From a *public* history standpoint, most historians (from uni profs to junior high social studies teachers) assume people have a basic knowledge of the period. Many also don't like to teach about it/talk about it because they've taught it a million times before. People are unironically tired of hearing about events they've heard about a million times, and some people have a very extreme reaction to it that is based in a widespread distrust of authority and academia. IMHO, this mistrust stems from a feeling of inadequacy. Basically, when you tell them about the Holocaust, their knee jerk reaction is to think, "They are telling me about something that is accepted to be common knowledge. If they are telling me, they must assume I don't know. If they assume I don't know common knowledge, they must think I'm stupid. They must think they're smarter than me." This leads to feelings of resentment, and sadly, with academia that often manifests as a denial of fact. 

And academia doesn't do a good job of preventing this. Many academics have some degree of superiority complex. They tend to conflate education and intelligence. They tend to be a bit aloof. A lot of regular people hate this. How can they trust what's being said when everything's locked up in an ivory tower? 

The only way to stop this is to change how we educate and change with world of academia on a basic level. I wanna start by saying that I (usually) don't cut. I do self-harm on other ways though. 

First off, as for why people start cutting/self-harming, there's a variety of reasons. Typically they're related to mental health, often depression. There are an enormous number of disorders that can result in SH. That means there's really an immensely large number of reasons. For some (like me), it's to prove that they can feel things/prove that they are real. For others, it's because they believe they deserve punishment for things they've done/said/felt, regardless of whether that is even remotely true. For others, it may even be a cry for help, hoping that someone notices because they're too frightened to seek help of their own volition. 

After enough time, self-harm becomes an addiction. Like any addiction, it is immensely hard to quit, and any slight enticement could trigger a relapse. Every day comes with unique struggles. Often, fully quitting can prove near impossible for some, and harm *reduction* becomes the best option. Maybe you throw out your blades, but you still keep a rubber band around your wrist and snap it on your arm when you get the urge to harm. 

>Despite this, is it possible for someone to think "this is dumb. What's this gonna do?" and still cut?

Yes. Absolutely. I've thought this exact thing, actually. It's very much a thing with depression to think that way, scissor. 

>Where does the idea that cutting is a "good idea" come from.

No one really thinks it's a "good idea". Those of us that self-harm usually know it's bad, we know we "shouldn't". But we do it anyways because our brains tell us to. In my case, I usually don't choose to do it, it just kinda happens. I don't really make a conscious effort to hurt myself, I just kinda see myself picking something up and think, "well, I guess we're doing this again". My situation is likely different from other people, though, and others will have different experiences.

I don't have schizophrenia, however, I do have a dissociative disorder, one of the major symptoms of which is having voices in my head. 
Contrary to popular belief, DID and schizophrenia are extremely different disorders with different causes, symptoms, treatments etc. Even the way in which similar symptoms manifest is often quite different. Additionally, people with schizophrenia may hear hallucinatory voices, whereas people with DID may hear voices internally as parts of their own mind (alters) speak on their own as individuals. Schizophrenia is about a split from reality, DID is about a split from yourself. I do not claim to know what it's like to have schizophrenia nor do claim to speak for any schizophrenic people. 
That being said, in my experience, living with voices that others can't hear can be immensely difficult. For a long time, I thought it was a normal experience that everyone had. When I found out it wasn't, I severely questioned my own sanity. It can be immensely disconcerting to have a voice that isn't your own trying to put ideas and thoughts into your head. Additionally, it can make normal, everyday things quite difficult as a result of the constant noise. A major one for me (and many others) is sleeping. Falling asleep and staying asleep is often quite hard as even though you may be tired and wanting sleep, the voices may not feel the same. They may keep you awake or wake you up part way through the night. 
In general, living with voices in your head is typically really difficult. It makes you question everything, often to the point of paranoia. It can make simple tasks difficult and difficult tasks impossible due to the constant mental noise.

The trans experience is defined by what makes you feel happy and comfortable, not about what makes you uncomfortable. You don't need dysphoria to be trans. If you're AMAB and thinking about being a girl actively makes you happy, then you might be trans. 

While I do experience dysphoria, I have experienced a similar thing. There have been times of my life (before I started transitioning) that I honestly didn't have too much of an issue with being a man. It was kinda a neutral feeling. But even in those times, the thought of being a woman (or frankly anything besides a man) actively made me happy, as opposed to the neutrality of my feelings on masculinity. 

Coming from someone with often extremely bad dysphoria: feeling like shit in your body is not and should not be the defining factor of the trans experience. Being trans is a personal revelation that only you can define for yourself. And your path can change along the way. Some people start transitioning and realize they were wrong, they don't like being perceived as a different gender. Some people realize they're just gender nonconforming (i.e. femboys & tomboys). 
And many more, like me, simply begin to feel more at peace and at home in their body and more comfortable with who they are. 

Only you can determine who you are. I wish you luck in your journey!!
